text: A major drawback of cheminformatics is the large amount of information present in its datasets. In most cases, these data contain redundant instances that affect the analysis of similarity measurements in drug design and discovery. Classical methods, such as the Protein Data Bank and quantum mechanical calculations, are therefore insufficient because of the dimensionality of the search spaces. In this paper, we introduce a hybrid metaheuristic algorithm called CHHO-CS, which combines the Harris hawks optimizer (HHO) with two operators: cuckoo search (CS) and chaotic maps. The role of CS is to control the main position vectors of the HHO algorithm in order to balance the exploitation and exploration phases, while the chaotic maps update the control energy parameters to avoid local optima and premature convergence. Feature selection (FS) reduces the dimensionality of a dataset by removing redundant and undesired information, which makes it very useful in cheminformatics. FS methods employ a classifier to identify the best subset of features. In the proposed CHHO-CS, support vector machines (SVMs) serve as the objective function for the classification process in FS. The CHHO-CS-SVM approach is tested on the selection of appropriate chemical descriptors and compound activities. Various datasets are used to validate its efficiency, including ten from the UCI machine learning repository. In addition, two chemical datasets (quantitative structure-activity relationship biodegradation and monoamine oxidase) were used to select the most significant chemical descriptors and compound activities. Extensive experimental and statistical analyses show that the proposed CHHO-CS method achieved better trade-off solutions than competing algorithms from the literature, including HHO, CS, particle swarm optimization, moth-flame optimization, the grey wolf optimizer, the salp swarm algorithm, and the sine-cosine algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate that the complexity associated with cheminformatics can be handled by using chaotic maps and hybridizing metaheuristic methods.

The Ascend West and Central Africa programme, funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), supports integrated preventative chemotherapy for up to five neglected tropical diseases (NTDs): intestinal worms, lymphatic filariasis, river blindness, trachoma and schistosomiasis. The programme is implemented across 13 countries by a consortium of four leading international development partners: Sightsavers, the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative Foundation and Mott MacDonald. This paper presents lessons learnt from country assessments carried out before the global outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). These lessons remain relevant after COVID-19, as national NTD programmes now face the added challenge of continuing to deliver mass drug administration (MDA) during the pandemic. Since the earliest stages of the pandemic, stakeholders have coordinated at two levels: in the first mile, with global partners of the NTD Supply Chain Forum, and in the last mile, with implementing partners in each country. This coordination has been instrumental in managing delayed MDA, including the effect of delays on the shipment of donated NTD drugs and on the distribution of stock held in country. The Ascend West and Central Africa programme is supporting countries to resume MDA through a risk assessment and mitigation action (RAMA) process.

Background: Quality-assured medicines are a principal means of achieving the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. The Global Drug Facility (GDF) of the Stop TB Partnership, the largest provider of tuberculosis (TB) medicines to the public sector worldwide, offers an example of quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) procedures in drug procurement.

Methods: The procedures and results of the GDF's QA/QC over the five-year period 2013-2017 were analysed retrospectively. Within this period, 13,999 batches of 51 different medicines were procured and reviewed, and 1,388 of these batches were analysed in the laboratories of the GDF's external quality control agent (QCA). Assay and dissolution results determined by the manufacturers and by the external QCA were compared using Bland-Altman analysis.

Results: All investigated batches of medicines were within specifications at the time of shipment. QA/QC costs were 0.8% of purchase costs, and the median time required for chemical analysis was 10 working days. For the poorly water-soluble compound rifampicin, the comparison showed a bias of 4.4%, with manufacturers reporting higher values than the external QCA, most likely because of the different analytical methods employed. Overall, the 95% limits of agreement (LOAs) were -6.7 to +8.0% for assay and -10.1 to +11.8% for dissolution. For kanamycin injections, the 95% LOAs for assay reached -14.5 to +13.2%, largely because of samples from one manufacturer that used a microbiological assay while the external QCA used an HPLC assay.

Conclusions: The GDF's procedures are a useful benchmark for evaluating the QA/QC procedures of other medicine procurement operations. Inter-laboratory comparison using Bland-Altman plots makes it possible to investigate bias and variability in medicine quality control. Drug procurement agencies should consider it a routine procedure to identify priorities for further improvement.

Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), caused by a genetic mutant of feline enteric coronavirus known as FIPV, is a highly fatal disease of cats for which there is currently no vaccine or FDA-approved cure. Dissemination of FIPV in affected cats results in a range of clinical signs, including cavitary effusions, anorexia, fever, and lesions of pyogranulomatous vasculitis and perivasculitis, with or without central nervous system and/or ocular involvement. There is a critical need for effective, approved antiviral therapies against coronaviruses, including FIPV and zoonotic coronaviruses such as SARS-CoV-2, the cause of COVID-19. Regarding SARS-CoV-2, preliminary evidence suggests potential clinical and pathological overlap with feline coronaviral disease, including enteric and neurological involvement in some cases. We screened 89 putative antiviral compounds and identified 25 with antiviral activity against FIPV, representing a variety of drug classes and mechanisms of antiviral action. Building on successful combination treatment strategies for human patients with HIV or hepatitis C virus infections, we identified combinations of drugs targeting different steps of the FIPV life cycle that produced a synergistic antiviral effect. In translational terms, we suggest that a combined anticoronaviral therapy (cACT) with multiple mechanisms of action and penetration of all potential anatomic sites of viral infection should be applied to other hard-to-treat coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV-2.

Author summary: We screened 89 compounds in vitro for antiviral activity against FIPV. The putative antiviral activity of these compounds was thought to arise either from a direct effect on viral proteins involved in replication or from an indirect inhibitory effect on normal cellular pathways that FIPV usurps to aid its replication. Twenty-five of these compounds showed significant antiviral activity. Certain combinations of them were found to be superior to monotherapy alone.

The integration of human rights principles into sexual and reproductive health (SRH) research is often recognised as valuable. Good examples abound, but there is still a lack of clarity about what defines rights-inclusive SRH research. To help move the field forward, this article explores how key stakeholders responsible for funding and supporting rights in SRH research understand the strengths and weaknesses of current practice and where it is being done, and it begins to catalogue potential tools and actions for the future. We conducted and analysed interviews with a range of key stakeholders, including international civil servants, donors and researchers who are committed to and supportive of integrating rights into SRH research. The interviews confirmed important differences in what is understood to be SRH rights-oriented research and in what it can accomplish. General barriers include a lack of understanding of the importance of rights, a lack of clarity about the best approach to integration, a fear of adding more work with little added benefit, and a lack of methodological guidance or published research methodologies that integrate rights. Suggestions include developing a comprehensive checklist for each phase of research, from drafting a research statement through to publication; developing training modules and workshops; including rights in curricula; changing journal requirements; and reaching agreement among key funders to mandate the integration of rights principles in the research proposals they receive. As a next step, cataloguing issues and concerns at the local level can help move the integration of human rights in SRH research from rhetoric to reality.

Background: Systems thinking is a conceptual approach that can help stakeholders understand complexity and make progress on persistent public health challenges. Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), a complex global health problem, are responsible for a large disease burden among impoverished populations around the world. The aim of this study was to better discern the many complexities of the global NTD system in order to identify and act on leverage points that can catalyse progress towards ending NTDs.

Methods: Existing frameworks for systems change were adapted to form the conceptual framework for the study. Using a semi-structured interview guide, we conducted key informant interviews with NTD stakeholders at the global level and at the country level in Nigeria. The interview data were coded and analysed to create causal loop diagrams, which resulted in a qualitative model of the global NTD system.

Results: The complete qualitative model is discussed and presented visually as six separate sub-components that highlight key forces and feedback loops within the global NTD system.

Conclusions: We identified five leverage points for NTD system change: (1) clarify the potential for, and assess realistic progress towards, NTD elimination; (2) increase support for interventions other than drug delivery; (3) reduce dependency on international donors; (4) create a less insular culture within the global NTD community; and (5) systematically address the issue of health worker incentives. The specific findings for NTDs raise a number of uncomfortable questions that have not been addressed, at least in part because it is easier to keep focusing on 'quick win' solutions. The study provides a model of a systems thinking approach that can be applied to other complex global health and development challenges to understand complexity and identify leverage points for system change.

Background: The Benishangul-Gumuz region is an important development corridor in Ethiopia. Large-scale projects such as the Great Renaissance Dam, mining and agriculture have entailed major environmental modifications and changes in settlement patterns. No detailed epidemiological information on visceral leishmaniasis (VL) exists for the region.

Materials and methods: A cross-sectional study was carried out to assess the epidemiology of, and risk factors associated with, Leishmania infection. A leishmanin skin test (LST) was performed on 1342 participants, and rK39 and DAT tests were performed on 253 of them. Thirty-six dogs owned by households with LST-positive member(s) were also tested with rK39 and DAT. A pretested questionnaire was used to capture individual and household characteristics.

Results: Of the 89.2% (1197/1342) of participants who presented for LST reading, 6.0% were positive. Among the 253 people tested, rK39 and DAT positivity were 3.2% and 5.9%, respectively. In dogs, positivity rates by rK39 and DAT were 13.9% and 5.6%, respectively. Among the household and individual risk factors, the presence of a dog in the household (P = 0.005), male sex (P = 0.003), residence woreda (P = 0.000) and occupation (P = 0.023) showed a strong positive association with LST positivity. Individuals living in households with dogs were 2.6 times more likely to be LST positive (AOR = 2.6; 95% CI = 1.54, 4.40). Being female decreased the probability of being LST positive by a factor of 0.38 (AOR = 0.38; 95% CI = 0.20, 0.72). People living in Guba and Kurmuk had 4.7 (AOR = 4.74, 95% CI 1.83, 12.31) and 5.9 (AOR = 5.85, 95% CI 2.27, 15.09) times higher risk of infection, respectively.

Conclusions: We demonstrated active VL transmission in these areas. We therefore underline the need to identify the responsible vector(s) and reservoir(s) in order to develop comprehensive early containment plans and prevent potentially harmful public health and economic consequences.

Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a highly infectious zoonotic virus that was first reported in the human population in September 2012 on the Arabian Peninsula. The virus causes severe and often lethal respiratory illness in humans, with an unusually high fatality rate. The N-terminal domain (NTD) of the receptor-binding S1 subunit of coronavirus spike (S) proteins can recognize a variety of host proteins and mediates entry into human host cells. Blocking entry by targeting the S1-NTD of the virus could facilitate the development of effective antiviral drug candidates against the pathogen. This study was therefore designed to identify effective antiviral drug candidates against MERS-CoV by targeting the S1-NTD. First, a structure-based pharmacophore model (SBPM) was generated for the active site (AS) cavity of the S1-NTD, followed by pharmacophore-based virtual screening of 11,295 natural compounds. The hits from the virtual screening were re-ranked by molecular docking and further evaluated through their ADMET properties. Compounds with the best ADME and toxicity properties were retrieved, and quantum mechanical (QM) density-functional theory (DFT) was used to optimize the geometry of the selected compounds. Three optimized natural compounds, namely Taiwanhomoflavone B (Amb23604132), 2,3-Dihydrohinokiflavone (Amb23604659), and Sophoricoside (Amb1153724), showed substantial docking energies of >-9.00 kcal/mol, and frontier molecular orbital (FMO) analysis found low chemical reactivity corresponding to the bioactivity of the compounds. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation confirmed the stability of the selected natural compounds at the binding site of the protein. In addition, molecular mechanics generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) calculations predicted good binding free energies (ΔG bind) for the compounds to the target protein. Taken together, the results support the potential of the selected compounds as natural antiviral candidates against the MERS-CoV S1-NTD.

Muscle atrophy is a side effect of several terrestrial diseases, and it also severely affects astronauts on space missions because of the reduced gravity in spaceflight. We present an integrative, graph-theoretic, network-based drug repurposing methodology that quantifies the interplay of key gene regulation and protein-protein interactions in muscle atrophy conditions. Transcriptomic datasets from mice in spaceflight, obtained from GeneLab, were extensively mined to extract the key genes that cause muscle atrophy in organ muscle tissues such as the thymus, liver, and spleen. The top muscle atrophy gene regulators were selected by the Bayesian Markov blanket method, and a gene-disease knowledge graph was constructed using the Scalable Precision Medicine Knowledge Engine. A deep graph neural network was trained to predict links in the network. The top-ranked diseases were identified, and drugs for repurposing were selected using the DrugBank resource. A disease-drug knowledge graph was then constructed, and the graph neural network was trained to predict new drugs. The results were compared with those of machine learning methods such as random forest and gradient boosting classifiers. Network-measure-based methods showed that preferential attachment performs well for link prediction in both the gene-disease and disease-drug graphs. The receiver operating characteristic curves and prediction accuracies for each method show that the random walk similarity measure and the deep graph neural network outperform the other methods. Several key target genes identified by the graph neural network are associated with diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and neural disorders. Applied to the disease-drug knowledge graph, the novel link prediction approach identifies monoclonal antibody therapy as a suitable candidate for drug repurposing for spaceflight-induced microgravity. A total of 21 drugs were identified as possible candidates for treating muscle atrophy. The graph neural network is a promising deep learning architecture for link prediction in gene-disease and disease-drug networks.

The Hippo pathway is an important signaling pathway that modulates growth control and cancer cell proliferation. Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway is a common feature of several types of cancer cells. Modulating the interaction between yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional enhanced associate domain (TEAD) in the Hippo pathway is considered an attractive target for cancer therapeutic development, although inhibiting this protein-protein interaction (PPI) is challenging. To investigate the hot spots of the YAP-TEAD1 interacting complex, we introduced an ab initio fragment molecular orbital (FMO) method. Using these hot spots, we constructed pharmacophores for inhibitor design and then performed virtual screening of an in-house library. Next, we performed molecular docking simulations and FMO calculations on the screening results to study the binding modes and affinities between PPI inhibitors and TEAD1. The virtual screening yielded three virtual hit compounds. To confirm their biological activities, we performed cellular assays (luciferase activity, proximity ligation assay and wound healing assay in A375 cells, and qRT-PCR in HEK 293T cells) and biophysical assays (surface plasmon resonance). Based on the findings of the study, we propose a novel PPI inhibitor, BY03, and demonstrate a profitable strategy for analyzing the YAP-TEAD PPI and discovering novel PPI inhibitors.

The increasing number of infections caused by antibiotic-resistant strains of pathogens challenges modern drug discovery technologies. Combinatorial chemistry approaches are based on chemical libraries. They enable the creation of high-affinity, low-molecular-weight ligands for therapeutically significant molecular targets of human cells, thus opening an avenue toward the directed design of highly effective therapeutic agents. Nevertheless, these approaches face insurmountable difficulties in antibiotic discovery. Natural compounds, which have evolved for such important characteristics as broad specificity and efficiency, are a good alternative to chemical libraries. However, the unrestricted use of natural antibiotics and their analogues leads to an avalanche-like spread of resistance among bacteria. The search for new natural antibiotics is in turn made extremely complicated by the problem of antibiotic rediscovery. This calls for alternative high-throughput platforms for screening antibiotic activity, the cultivation of "unculturable" microorganisms, the exploration of novel antibiotic biosynthetic gene clusters, and their activation and heterologous expression. Microfluidic technologies for screening antibiotic activity at the level of single cells are therefore of great interest, because they allow a single platform to combine ultrahigh-throughput screening, next-generation sequencing, and genome mining, opening up unique opportunities for antibiotic discovery.

The performance of quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models depends largely on the relevance of the molecular representation selected as the input data matrix. This work presents a thorough comparative analysis of two main categories of molecular representations (vector space and metric space) for fitting robust machine learning models to QSAR problems. To assess these methods, seven molecular representations were evaluated: RDKit descriptors, five types of fingerprints (MACCS, PubChem, FP2-based, Atom Pair, and ECFP4), and a graph matching approach (non-contiguous atom matching structure similarity; NAMS), in both vector space and metric space. They were subjected to state-of-the-art machine learning methods, including different dimensionality reduction methods (feature selection and linear dimensionality reduction). Five distinct QSAR data sets were used for direct assessment and analysis. The results show that, in general, metric-space and vector-space representations can produce equivalent models, but there are significant differences between individual approaches. The NAMS-based similarity approach consistently outperformed most fingerprint representations in model quality, followed closely by Atom Pair fingerprints. To further verify these findings, the metric-space-based models were fitted to the same data sets with the closest neighbors removed. These later results further strengthened the conclusions above. The graph-based metric-space approach appeared significantly superior to the other representations, albeit at a significant computational cost.

The four rare neurodegenerative diseases taken as examples in this study clearly highlight the limited availability of approved therapies for the management of rare pathologies, underscoring the importance of drug repurposing approaches for filling these gaps. Indeed, drug repurposing appears to be a cost- and time-saving procedure in the research and development of orphan drugs. Identifying repurposed drugs with potential therapeutic benefit involves experimental or in silico approaches that depend on a good understanding of the molecular disease mechanisms, which highlights the key role of fundamental research in the process. In recent years, the use of patient stem cell-based high-throughput screening approaches and in silico prediction tools, such as network mapping, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and rare variant association studies (RVAS), has significantly accelerated the identification of candidate drugs for disease treatment. Despite these advances, which have helped identify promising drugs for the treatment of different rare diseases, including HD, FRDA, Wolfram syndrome, and ALS, an important translational gap remains between the volume of preclinical and clinical research conducted and the number of repurposed drugs that gain approval. This gap results from several factors. Clinical trials in rare diseases are difficult to organize because of the small number of patients, their wide geographical distribution, their short life span, and the severity of the diseases, all of which complicate study design and the determination of relevant clinical endpoints. There are also ethical concerns about introducing a placebo group into the trial: if one is present, it may discourage patients from participating, and if it is absent, the validity of the trial is reduced. Moreover, the high rate of late-stage failure of clinical studies, as observed for the rare neurodegenerative diseases described in this article, is another important factor contributing to the small number of approved repurposed drugs. HD, Wolfram syndrome, FRDA, and ALS are largely heterogeneous diseases of varying severity. Clinical trials performed in large, heterogeneous patient cohorts have often failed to demonstrate the benefits of the drugs under investigation despite very promising preclinical and pilot clinical data. This points to the need for better clinical trial designs that evaluate drug effects in specific patient cohorts, as highlighted by several post hoc data analyses.

"Trying to engage the community without engaging the local health ministry was a non-starter completely... there were a lot of inducements that needed to be applied to the local policymakers, and it involved numerous meetings, numerous visits to the health ministry, basically trying to convince them that this is a good idea." (Workshop participant #1)

The workshop discussion also showed that community leaders were sometimes instrumental in creating barriers to working with the most marginalized communities. Gatekeepers may block researchers' entry for multiple reasons, which can be grounded in past experiences with international or other forms of health research where they live.

"...gatekeepers or leaders of communities may restrict access to the most marginalised members of the community. And I think that's absolutely true (...) But a lot of it is not being paternalistic, but they are sometimes advocating for those members and keeping them safe." (Workshop participant #2)

Some of the actors on whom researchers depend for permission to do their research in the community, particularly political actors, can also have a less benign side. Gatekeepers can therefore be barriers as well as people who facilitate access.

"I had to cancel one of my events, because I was working with one member of parliament coming from an opposition political party. And when the government noted that, they withdrew the police services to cover my event." (Workshop participant #7)

"To ensure long-term, sustainable change, the local community has to voice the local concerns and participate in defining the healthcare challenges. In turn, we aim for communities to develop a sense of responsibility and ownership of the solutions." (Unit #10 - from content analysis)

The excerpt above hints at the notion of the "legacy" of the research. We define "legacy" as a concept that synthesizes the ideas of sustainability and long-term impact: working toward long-term improvements that extend beyond the research lifecycle and create a sense of ownership of the research within communities.

The outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which causes coronavirus disease (COVID-19), has been declared a global pandemic. By September 2021, more than 220 million people had been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and more than 4.5 million of them had died. Antivirals targeting SARS-CoV-2, such as remdesivir, have modest clinical benefits, which indicates a need for more effective antivirals to complement anti-inflammatory therapy approaches for the treatment of COVID-19. The timeline for developing new drugs is about 10 years, and given the current dire need for effective antiviral agents, identifying new drugs with antiviral activity cannot provide antiviral therapies in time to address the current pandemic. Drug repurposing is the preferred method for developing rapid-response therapies, as it prioritizes the identification of additional drugs that can be repurposed as antivirals.

Repositioning of approved drugs can be achieved by repurposing a drug for a related disease, by repurposing a target with a known drug for another indication, or by repurposing a drug for a novel target through off-target interactions. The relative prevalence of the three approaches reflects the balance between their feasibility and the breadth of their applicability. The disease-centric approach, although the most direct and the most common, accounting for 59% of repositioning successes, has a narrower generalizability in the disease space, as exemplified by the modest utility of the repurposed antivirals described above. Target-centric repurposing has the potential for broader application as a less direct approach, but it is less common because the discovery of a novel link between a target and a disease is rare. Even when such a link is discovered, the generalizability of the target-centric approach is limited by drug-target coverage of the human proteome: as of 2019, only 667 of the roughly 20,000 human proteins (~3%) are directly targeted by FDA-approved drugs. For that reason, drug-centric repurposing, as the least direct methodology, offers access to a much broader range of repurposing opportunities. However, because it aims to find novel, off-target drug-target interactions and therefore relies on a fundamental understanding of structural information about both the drug and the target, it has been the least prevalent repositioning approach, accounting for only 6% of successes.

In the article submitted to eLife by Shin et al., the authors investigate the mechanisms of Acinetobacter baumannii resistance to polymyxin B. They isolate random mutations that arise in the genome as a result of culturing A. baumannii in media containing PMB, and they find isolates with low and high levels of PMB resistance. Whole genome sequencing identifies nearly 20 non-synonymous mutations in different genes. Substitutions in pmrB were common to two isolates. The authors generate deletion mutants and overexpression genotypes for PmrB, and they also construct deletions in the other genes. They then move on to characterize PmrB-dependent production of OMVs. The reason for focusing on this gene rather than the others is not firmly established. The data that follow are not conducted with a sufficient level of rigor to merit acceptance in this journal. No statistical analysis is presented, and the significance of the data is not established, which makes the impact of the study very minimal.

To my knowledge, the work demonstrating the involvement of PmrB in OMV formation for this important pathogen is novel and consistent with recent data suggesting that modified LOS molecules might promote or prevent vesicle formation. In general, the work is well written and easy to follow conceptually. However, the level of rigor applied to this study falls well short of the requirements for this journal. In its current form, the article does not have sufficient impact to warrant publication here.

Data on PMB resistance are presented as MICs and growth curve measurements. No bactericidal assay is used, which is a major weakness and oversight. The authors report no cfu data for the bacteria that were treated. The data are over-interpreted.

The authors do not use appropriate assays to assess whether the particles they are measuring are actual OMVs. Western blots and enzymatic assays for specific proteins that do or do not localize to OMVs are absent and must be included.

Summary: This is a well-written manuscript that provides novel insights into malaria-induced anemia. 2) A better effort is needed to incorporate recent developments in our understanding of what atypical/T-bet+ cells are. If atypical/T-bet+ cells are recently activated, optimally derived cells, then it follows that they are the main cells contributing to the circulating antibody pool in a recent infection (presumably after differentiating into antibody-secreting cells, which the study does not really mention). It makes sense that they would not produce much anti-DNA antibody, because presumably this has not been elicited recently (or at least is not the dominant recent stimulus).

This submission reports an approach to identify bacteria-specific carboxylesterases that can be exploited to activate antibiotic prodrugs in Staphylococcus aureus. The premise is that the charged functional groups found in some antibiotics prevent their entry into bacteria, an effect that can be circumvented by esterifying the antibiotic to allow entry. The antibiotic is then activated in the bacterial cytoplasm by hydrolysis by bacterial esterases. The study reports an interesting and generalisable approach to discovering prodrug-activating enzymes for use in developing new treatments for microbes.

1. The issue of resistance is not addressed sufficiently. This strategy relies on non-essential bacterial enzymes for drug activation, and bacteria could circumvent it by mutating the drug-activating enzymes. Dependence on microbial activation is always a liability, as has been shown for M. tuberculosis agents such as isoniazid and pyrazinamide. Ultimately this can be tested experimentally, for example by determining the resistance frequencies for HEX or another prodrug and comparing them with the frequencies for known antibiotics. This would strengthen the work and provide a more balanced view.

2. While serum esterase would clearly be a concern, there are also abundant esterases in the liver. No mention was made of stability in liver microsomes or, even better, hepatocytes, to give a picture of the overall metabolic stability of the leading pro-moieties.

3. There are few data on the effect of the ether group of the ester on activity, as the experiments were done using a fluorescence-based system. Some evidence that these selectivities extend to more real-world systems and antibiotics would be helpful.

3. The analysis cohort is not described at all, which is important, especially in the context of risk factors for ARDs and the history of ARDs.

4. Exposure to an infection is presented as the proportion of children with that infection per year, but not per child. For each infection, what was the incidence rate and its variability between children? It is unclear how exposure was captured for each child in the analysis, as an incidence or as 'at least one infection'. Incidence could have been a better representation of exposure.

6. It would be worth summarizing in the introduction the effects of the RCTs on allergy outcomes up to 9 years, so that the reader is informed of any potential effects of the treatment arms on the study outcomes, given that the analysis does not take the original design into account. It might also be worth performing subgroup analyses among the control arms of both RCTs to see whether the results, albeit likely underpowered, are consistent with the whole-group analysis, so that treatment allocations can be safely ignored. It would be useful to discuss in the limitations section the potential effects, if any, of these RCTs on the study findings.

7. The cohort comprises 2345 children, but only 1179 have data on ARD at nine years of age. As the goal is to investigate a possible association between early-life infection exposure and susceptibility to ARDs, shouldn't the total number of analyzed subjects be 1179? The authors should either repeat the LTA or discuss the difference in sample populations (2345 vs 1179) as a weakness or limitation of their study.

8. In describing the methodology for the ARD information, the authors state (page 6, lines 122-124) that they used 20-fold diluted plasma, which significantly reduces the sensitivity of their test. IgE tests are normally done on undiluted serum. The reason for diluting the plasma 20-fold should be given. Moreover, information on the validation of this assay against a gold standard (e.g., ImmunoCAP, TFS) should at least be mentioned here (a reference alone is not enough). Finally, what SPT wheal (not papule) diameter corresponds to the threshold of 312.5 ng/ml? Is the IgE test sensitive enough?

Subsection "Chromobody labelled F-actin structures disappear upon disruption of PfACT1". The authors say that disruption causes an apicoplast segregation defect as a consequence. I do not see this. In Figure 3F the apicoplast dots are smaller, but why would this be the case if the phenotype were a segregation defect?

Subsection "DiCre-mediated conditional disruption of Formin-2 causes a defect in apicoplast segregation in P. falciparum". The authors speak of collapsed or morphologically aberrant apicoplasts. All one can see is a series of dots, and nothing allows one to define a particular dot as a particular "type" of apicoplast. Again, there are no numbers, counts or statistics. What is a collapsed apicoplast, and what does it look like at a sensible resolution, i.e., using electron microscopy?

Previous work has shown that actin filaments are involved in apicoplast division, and this paper seeks to implicate Formin in that process. This is not an unexpected factor to be involved. For the paper to merit publication in such a journal, it would need a stronger functional message based on more quantitative microscopy, some statistical analysis and some biochemistry. The only reference cited after this sentence that mentions P. berghei is Brant et al., and there it is used as P. berghei ANKA, the sub-strain that causes experimental cerebral malaria (ECM) in susceptible mice. P. berghei NK65, another sub-strain that is very closely related to P. berghei ANKA, never results in ECM. Please use the full strain name, P. berghei ANKA.

Stress, including drug-induced stress, is known to stimulate sexual conversion in P. falciparum, so the conceptual novelty is somewhat limited. While the meaning of such a phenomenon in a clinical context remains unclear, the data are solid, and this study provides a novel tool for investigating the signaling pathways that lead to sexual conversion.

A main novel finding here is that ring stages of Pf are refractory to sexual conversion following drug and metabolic changes. DHA arrests ring stages before killing them, so DHA-treated rings might require a longer latent period before conversion to gametocytes. The authors should measure conversion at least 24-48 hours later than their measurement for DHA-treated trophozoites. In Figure 2, did the authors test other concentrations of DHA on rings? Since they show that the DHA effect at the trophozoite stage is dose-dependent, one may expect DHA to affect sexual conversion at the ring stage at concentrations higher than 10 nM.

It is not clear how and when the total percentage of gametocytes was measured following drug treatments (data presented in Figure 1E and Figure 2E), or whether DHA increases both the proportion of early gametocytes and their subsequent development into mature gametocytes after 10-14 days, or whether the increase was driven merely by a reduction in asexual forms or by increased RBC lysis following drug exposure. In this study, and in the previous article by Portugaliza et al. (2019), the authors define the sexual conversion rate as the proportion of parasites that convert into sexual forms in each replicative cycle, which can be estimated as the gametocytemia divided by the initial parasitemia. This is indeed how the authors calculated the sexual conversion rate when using the NF54-10.3-Tom line (measured by dividing the gametocytemia on day 3 (D3) by the initial ring-stage parasitemia on D0). However, when using the NF54-gexp02-Tom reporter line, the authors used a different calculation (subsection "Determination of sexual conversion rates"): "the sexual conversion rate was calculated as the sexual stage parasitemia divided by the total (sexual + asexual) parasitemia, and expressed as percentage". This corresponds to the proportion of gametocytes and not exactly to the sexual conversion rate, which is over-estimated when the number of asexual parasites is reduced by the effects of the drug. Therefore, the axis labels in graphs 1D, 2D, 3B, 4B, 5C, etc. should be changed to something like "proportion of gametocytes". The authors should consider using a more accurate calculation of sexual conversion, as they did in their 2019 paper with the NF54-gexp02-Tom parasites or in this study with NF54-10.3-Tom.

DESCRIPTION (provided by applicant): Host variation affects the pathogenicity of, susceptibility to, and recovery from infectious diseases. Elucidating how the host environment alters antibiotic susceptibility is therefore a critical step toward the long-term goal of realizing precision medicine for the clinical management of infectious diseases. The overall objective of this project is to identify the metabolic pathways that participate in antibiotic susceptibility and to determine how host metabolism may affect antibiotic treatment at the site of infection. The working hypothesis is that metabolic processes can function as bacterial control mechanisms for antibiotic susceptibility and that the host metabolome can act on these processes to affect the outcome of antibiotic treatment. This hypothesis will be tested in three specific aims: (1) identify metabolic pathways involved in antibiotic susceptibility (K99 phase); (2) characterize changes in the host metabolome elicited by antibiotic administration (K99 phase); and (3) evaluate the effects of the host metabolome on antibiotic killing (R00 phase). During the mentored K99 phase, bactericidal antibiotics will be counterscreened with various metabolites to identify metabolic perturbations that can affect antibiotic susceptibility. Metabolic pathways contributing to antibiotic lethality will be identified by combining these data with metabolic modeling and machine learning. In addition, plasma and peritoneal fluid will be sampled and metabolomically profiled in a mouse peritoneal infection model, with and without antibiotic treatment. These profiles will be used to determine whether antibiotics can alter host metabolism in ways that may affect antibiotic susceptibility at the site of infection. During the independent R00 phase, the effects of host metabolic variation on antibiotic killing will be systematically tested by quantifying antibiotic susceptibility in synthesized media defined by metabolomic profiles from published and measured human and mouse plasma samples. A better understanding of how the host metabolic environment participates in antibiotic treatment fits NIH's public health mission and has direct implications for the clinical management of infectious diseases. The proposed studies will form a quantitative framework for directly evaluating how host metabolism may affect antibiotic treatment outcomes and for guiding improved antibiotic stewardship in clinical practice. Although the applicant has significant expertise in systems biology, this award will provide research training to gain new experimental skills, as well as an opportunity for continued career training and mentorship from an advisory committee composed of international leaders in systems biology, metabolomics, chemical biology and infectious diseases. The support and training provided by this award and by the advisory committee will give the applicant the tools and expertise critical to his future independent research program.

Project summary. This is a comprehensive application to support training in malaria surveillance, epidemiology and implementation science research in order to strengthen malaria policy and control in Uganda. Although Uganda has dramatically scaled up the available malaria control interventions, the burden of malaria remains very high, and the optimal strategies for controlling malaria in this high-transmission setting are still unclear. New interventions or new delivery approaches are needed to have a sustained impact on reducing the disease burden. Expertise in malaria research remains limited in Uganda, which makes additional training necessary.

In 1998, a collaborative malaria research project was established between Makerere U and the University of California, San Francisco. In 2010, our research program was awarded the East African International Center of Excellence for Malaria Research (ICEMR) award, whose goal is to perform comprehensive surveillance studies aimed at improving understanding of the disease and measuring the impact of population-level control interventions. This program has expanded our already outstanding set of research training opportunities. To date, our training programs have largely focused on the master's level, with few trainees at the doctoral level or in a position to influence policy. Our previous training has thus created a large pool of candidates who are suitable for doctoral-level training and able to lead a new generation of scientists in translating research into policy.

For Ugandan expertise in malaria control to grow and diversify, we propose to establish a comprehensive research training program at Makerere University School of Medicine focused on strengthening malaria control and policy in Uganda. Our objectives are to: 1) substantially increase the scientific leadership and expertise needed for independent malaria epidemiology, surveillance and implementation science research; 2) strengthen the capabilities and career development of junior faculty at Makerere U to lead, manage and train students in malaria research, by providing postdoctoral mentored research training; 3) strengthen the sustainability of malaria research at Makerere U by strengthening the Makerere U malaria research center; and 4) promote collaboration between the National Malaria Control Program and malaria research programs in Uganda to foster evidence-based decision making.

The collaborators on the ICEMR and other research grants provide a pool of faculty who will ensure high-quality supervision and mentoring of trainees. Degree trainees will be registered at Makerere U or the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and non-degree long- and short-term training will take place in Uganda and at UCSF. Given the changing malaria epidemiology in Uganda and the potential for sustainable malaria research-to-policy activities in the country, we are ideally positioned to strengthen the capacity for malaria research and control in Uganda. We anticipate training 4 PhD candidates, 5 candidates in master's degree programs, 9 candidates in long-term non-degree training and over 100 candidates in short-term non-degree programs.

Low-cost sequencing has ushered in a new era of drug discovery that can use genomic information from hundreds of thousands of people. However, humans are a limited resource for identifying novel drug targets, and attempts at therapeutic development often rely on an already well-known set of genes and pathways. Greater potential for discovery exists if we broaden our search across the animal kingdom. In particular, animal adaptations for disease resistance have great potential to uncover novel biological pathways to counteract human diseases. Hibernating mammals are an especially rich resource for inspiring novel therapeutics, as they exhibit numerous transient phenotypes that mirror critical human health problems, such as ischemia-reperfusion injury, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis, muscle atrophy, and obesity/diabetes, yet they are able to avoid or reverse the associated pathologies.

A systematic understanding of the gene networks used to generate the protective and healing phenotypes of hibernators has great potential to reveal novel therapeutic avenues. However, targets that reproduce across independent datasets, including those associated with the same phenotype across multiple species, are more likely to translate to humans. In this proposal, we specifically propose to (1) obtain high-throughput phenotypic data to test our platform, (2) create a better model for identifying targets based on machine learning, and (3) extend our approach to new disease areas. Our long-term vision is to develop a genomics discovery platform centered on hibernating animals for all of the diseases discussed above. We believe that our approach will identify novel therapeutic targets that translate to humans, and we will advance our discoveries through strategic pharmaceutical partnerships.

MEDICINAL AND SYNTHETIC CHEMISTRY CORE

The Medicinal and Synthetic Chemistry Core (ChemCore) is a shared resource facility that provides chemistry services to enable translational programs to advance small molecule candidates from chemical biology to drug discovery. ChemCore supports investigators of the Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center (LCC), Northwestern University, and external organizations by providing advanced cheminformatics and chemical synthesis services. Cheminformatics uses many techniques and tools to perform computational chemistry, molecular modeling, and computer-aided drug design. This service gives investigators unique insights into the design of molecules that are active in cancer biology and guides the selection of candidates that can be synthesized and evaluated for their biological activities. Chemical synthesis gives researchers access to high-level resources for the custom synthesis of molecular probes and tools, compounds, hit-to-lead chemistry, lead optimization medicinal chemistry, and consulting on drug discovery projects.

The ChemCore's scientific team consists of PhD-level staff chemists with significant experience in pharmaceutical drug discovery. The facility is equipped with modern medicinal chemistry equipment and advanced computational and visualization resources that enable industry-level projects spanning the early stages of drug discovery through lead optimization. The daily interaction of computational and medicinal chemists with cancer biologists and clinicians is an essential feature of the core and has contributed to the success of translational projects at the LCC. We have engaged LCC investigators to forge new interdisciplinary research projects and pursue molecular medicine opportunities.

During the current funding period, 47 LCC members used ChemCore services to investigate the interactions between small molecules and biological systems. We have synthesized and tested more than 1,000 new compounds for nearly 30 different cancer therapeutic projects. ChemCore works closely with several other LCC-supported cores, particularly the High Throughput Analysis Laboratory (to identify "hits" through high-throughput screening campaigns) and the Developmental Therapeutics Core (to evaluate small molecule candidates in appropriate animal models). The long-range goal of ChemCore is to serve as one of the principal conduits through which LCC investigators translate their basic research into new therapeutics.

Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a mosquito-transmitted neglected tropical disease (NTD) that affects over 120 million people living in 72 countries. Current control strategies for LF, which rely on annual mass drug administration (MDA) to at-risk populations, have failed to interrupt disease transmission, partly because of chronic reinfection. No licensed prophylactic vaccine is currently available for LF, and few of those tested over the last two decades have advanced beyond rodent testing. This is partly because of poor protection, but also because of a lack of resources to advance the technology, given the truly neglected nature of the disease.

We have developed and established the first successful multivalent recombinant fusion protein (Bm-HAXT) for the prophylaxis of LF, called LFGuard(TM). This vaccine comprises a protein antigen, Bm-HAXT, formulated with the TLR4 agonist GLA-on-Alum. When formulated, our vaccine is highly stable and provides nearly sterile immunity in rodents (>95%) and significant protection in non-human primates (70%). To date, LFGuard(TM) has been extensively tested, and its prophylactic potential and safety have been confirmed in different animal models, such as mice (n=980), Mongolian gerbils (jirds) (n=220), and rhesus macaques (n=60). In addition to LF, LFGuard(TM) has also shown significant promise in dogs as a vaccine for heartworms.

This SBIR Phase 2 proposal will allow us to move LFGuard(TM) into pre-clinical development, including GMP manufacture, vialing, and stability and efficacy testing. A clinical study and a supporting toxicology study will be designed, and stability will be confirmed through both short- and long-term stability programs. Finally, we will conduct a pre-IND meeting with the FDA before executing the toxicology study. Once these studies are complete, this important antigen will be poised to enter the first human clinical trials for the first-ever lymphatic filariasis vaccine. We propose the following aims for this SBIR Phase 2 grant: (1) manufacture Bm-HAXT under cGMP, and (2) perform pre-clinical IND-enabling studies.

Malaria remains one of the most deadly diseases in the world, killing nearly a million people each year. Malaria is hard to control because the immunogenicity of malaria pathogens is very poor, which has made it difficult to generate anti-malaria vaccines. The rapid spread of insecticide resistance in mosquito populations and of drug resistance in Plasmodium parasites further increases the rate of malaria transmission. There is therefore a critical need for novel approaches to malaria control. Because malaria transmission depends on Plasmodium-infected mosquitoes, inhibiting parasite infection in mosquitoes represents a novel and practical way to break the transmission cycle. At present, most transmission-blocking studies focus on parasite gametocytes in blood and have had limited success, because gametocytes are strongly resistant to drugs. Very few efforts, however, have been made to use compounds against mosquito proteins to block malaria transmission.

We recently identified the FREP1 gene in wild An. gambiae from malaria-endemic areas in Kenya through association studies. Molecular and biochemical analyses revealed that the FREP1 protein mediates the invasion of multiple species of Plasmodium parasites in mosquito midguts through direct interaction with the parasites. Based on these findings, we developed a new high-throughput platform to screen a library of natural fungal extracts targeting FREP1, which enabled our team to identify a bioactive compound named P-orlandin that significantly inhibits P. falciparum infection in mosquitoes. Based on these preliminary studies, we hypothesize that small compounds that interfere with the malaria-mosquito interaction will inhibit malaria transmission.

Because multiple pathways are involved in Plasmodium invasion in mosquitoes, the overarching goal of this application is to develop a novel and effective approach that uses multiple fungal natural products to block malaria transmission by targeting multiple mosquito proteins that mediate parasite invasion. We will use our successful collaborative studies as a springboard for identifying additional targets that mediate parasite transmission, as well as small molecules that disrupt the process of malaria transmission. The compounds we find will not only serve as potential leads for field applications but also as essential chemical probes to dissect the molecular biology of the novel pathways we uncover.

In this study, we will identify additional candidate genes through genomic-block assistant-associated studies and verify their functional relationship with P. falciparum infection in mosquitoes. The candidate gene products that promote Plasmodium infection in mosquitoes will be chosen as targets to screen for small-molecule compounds that block malaria transmission. This work will provide bioactive compounds that are leads for the development of drugs or spray reagents to block malaria transmission. In addition, it will give the malaria community new mechanistic insight into Plasmodium transmission to mosquitoes at the molecular level.

Overuse of antibiotics in all settings accelerates the development of antibiotic resistance, a top threat to global health. Optimizing antibiotic use is a strategy for combatting resistance. Inter-hospital comparison of antibiotic use is recommended by national antibiotic stewardship implementation policies but requires accurate measurement of that use. Newborn infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) have high rates of antibiotic exposure. The purpose of this pharmacoepidemiology study is to provide a framework for safely optimizing neonatal antibiotic use. The project's specific aims are (1) to develop a risk-adjusted method for benchmarking antibiotic use across NICUs; (2) to develop a neonatal antibiotic use metric that accounts for the antibiotic spectrum of activity; and (3) to determine the associations between antibiotic use metrics and neonatal outcomes. Aims 1-3 will use neonatal data from the Premier Health Database, and Aims 2 and 3 will also use University of Pennsylvania patient-level neonatal data for validation. This study will directly address a top AHRQ research priority, promoting appropriate antibiotic use in order to reduce the transmission of resistant bacteria. The proposal focuses exclusively on newborn infants, an AHRQ priority population. The results of this research will identify meaningful metrics of neonatal antibiotic use, allowing hospitals and stakeholders to pinpoint antibiotic utilization practices that should be emulated or avoided, and ultimately improving the safety and quality of neonatal care.

This career development award is designed to support the transition of Dr. Dustin Flannery, an Instructor of Pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania and Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, into an independent physician-scientist and to help him achieve his long-term career goal of becoming a national expert in neonatal antibiotic stewardship and a leader in pediatric health services research. In addition, this award will allow him to obtain the training, mentorship, and research experience necessary to compete successfully for R01 grants supporting studies in this area.

Dr. Flannery will receive advanced training and experiential learning in pharmacoepidemiology research methods, advanced biostatistical techniques, and health services and policy. The University of Pennsylvania and Children's Hospital of Philadelphia provide a stellar research environment for conducting such research. The project will be guided by a renowned mentorship team with a track record of successful collaboration and scholarship, including experts in neonatology, infectious diseases, pharmacoepidemiology, health services, biostatistics, and outcomes research.

Globally, more than 90% of all snakebite envenomation (SBE) occurs in low-resource settings. This neglected tropical disease affects 2.7 million people and causes 81,000-138,000 deaths and approximately 400,000 permanent disabilities annually. Antivenom is a safe, efficacious, time-dependent, and evidence-based treatment, but the availability of this standard of care, and timely access to it, is inadequate. It is critical to engage local communities to improve timely access in the remote, low-resource areas where most SBE morbidity occurs.

This proposal will develop and evaluate an innovative multi-modal intervention to improve SBE care, including decentralized antivenom distribution through the existing community healthcare center (CHC) network in the Brazilian Amazon. This novel intervention will integrate (a) advanced geospatial artificial intelligence to create decentralized antivenom distribution models that use existing CHCs and optimize population coverage and time to reach care, (b) a cost-effectiveness evaluation model developed with key stakeholders, and (c) a culturally relevant SBE care package containing education, treatment guidelines, training on antivenom delivery, and interfacility care coordination. Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, we will conduct a formative evaluation of this multi-modal intervention and prepare an implementation strategy for the Brazilian Amazon, as well as prepare to scale up to other low-resource locations. As a result, we will have a standardized approach for using advanced analytics to optimize healthcare delivery in low-resource settings, which can be applied in other countries and to other healthcare interventions.

SickleGenAfrica is a genomics network that aims to test the overarching hypothesis that genetic variation in cytoprotective defenses against hemolysis influences the risk of organ damage in sickle cell disease (SCD). The focus of project 2 is to determine the genome-wide determinants of the risk of malaria complications in SCD.

Background of the project: Malaria in SCD is associated with severe complications and an increased risk of mortality. Hemolysis is a key process that contributes to the pathogenetic processes in both malaria and SCD, particularly with respect to acute and chronic end-organ damage leading to severe anemia and lung and brain injury. The four SickleGenAfrica countries (Ghana, Tanzania, Nigeria and Cameroon) and the US collaborators (Pittsburgh and Morehouse) have experience and expertise in both conditions and intend to use established resources to interrogate the two conditions, as well as to establish a murine model to evaluate malaria in SCD.

Specific aims: (1) To characterize the phenotype of severe malaria in SCD patients and determine the relationship between variations in HCP genes and malaria disease phenotype and severity. (2) To investigate the inflammatory response (cytokines/chemokines and adhesion molecules) in SCD patients with malaria and examine its relationship with HCP levels and the risk of severe malaria. (3) To functionally validate the association between HCPs and the severity of malaria in transgenic SCD mice.

The significance of the proposed research and its relevance to public health: SCD and malaria are both disorders of public health significance (annual SCD births of 300,000 globally; 3.3 billion people living in 106 countries at risk of malaria infection) with high mortality (up to 90% childhood mortality in SCD; 438,000 malaria deaths). Accurate description of disease expression and identification of genetic and environmental modifiers of disease will improve the diagnosis, management and prevention of malaria-related morbidity and mortality in SCD.

The unique features and innovation of the project: (1) It is the first study to investigate malaria in the largest SCD population (n=7,000). (2) It assesses the phenotypic description of malaria in SCD during the acute and steady states. (3) It evaluates the inflammatory response in malaria in SCD. (4) It uses a murine model to investigate malaria in SCD.

The methodology to be used: We will enrol 7,000 SCD patients in 4 countries at clinics and evaluate patients during hospitalization. We will infect transgenic SCD and control mice with Plasmodium, measure levels of hemolysis cytoprotective proteins and inflammatory markers, and evaluate disease expression, focusing on hemolysis and anemia as well as end-organ damage to the lung and brain.

Expected results and description of how the results will affect other research areas: A description of the phenotypic expression of the co-morbidity of malaria and SCD, with identification of genetic and environmental modifiers of disease, emphasizing the role of hemolysis in both conditions.

Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is the largest major surgical procedure by volume for Medicare, and infection is the largest reason for TKA revision. Irrigation and debridement (I&D) with long-term antibiotics is the preferred method for managing periprosthetic joint infection (PJI; infected TKA), but I&D fails in approximately 60% of cases. This high failure rate results from the formation of biofilm on the implant and the subsequent high tolerance of the biofilm to antibiotics. There is a large gap in knowledge about how biofilm develops antibiotic tolerance and how it is regulated, and there are no strategies to disrupt this tolerance in PJI.

The hypothesis of this proposal is that biofilm formation, regulated by toxin-antitoxin systems, is a major factor responsible for the formation of antibiotic-tolerant biofilm. In other chronic infections (i.e., tuberculosis and cystic fibrosis), biofilm formation and antibiotic tolerance are well recognized to decrease antibiotic efficacy. Understanding the initial events that lead to the development of antibiotic-tolerant biofilm in PJI is the first step in developing treatment strategies. The aims include establishing the relationship between biofilm formation and antibiotic tolerance. Preliminary results in this proposal demonstrate that biofilm formation is a critical step in the development of antibiotic-tolerant biofilm.

In Aim 1, we have collected a library of PJI clinical isolates and will identify genetic and phenotypic differences in binding and antibiotic-tolerant biofilm formation among these isolates. In Aim 2, we will determine the role of toxin-antitoxin systems in PJI biofilm formation and their association with antibiotic tolerance, both in vitro and in the animal model we have developed. This will add further evidence for the role of antibiotic-tolerant biofilm in PJI and help direct the development of improved treatment strategies.

A major factor plaguing drug development is the lack of a drug-screening tool that can distinguish drugs that will induce cardiac arrhythmias from chemically similar safe drugs. Current approaches rely on surrogate markers such as action potential duration or QT interval prolongation on the ECG. There is an urgent need for a new approach that can predict actual proarrhythmia from drug chemistry rather than relying on surrogate indicators. We have brought together an expert team to innovate at the interfaces of experimental and computational modeling disciplines and to develop an in silico simulation pipeline that predicts cardiotoxicity across multiple temporal and spatial scales, from the atom to the cardiac rhythm.

An essential and unique aspect of our approach is that we propose to use atomistic-scale simulation to predict the transition rates of ion channels and adrenergic receptors and how they are modified by drug interaction. We hypothesize that the subtleties of these interactions are likely to be the critical determinants of drug-associated safety or proarrhythmia. In the last award period, we successfully developed an unprecedented linkage: we connected the highly disparate space and time scales of ion channel structure and function. We used atomistic simulation to compute drug kinetic rates, which were directly used as parameters in a hERG functional model. The model components were then integrated into predictive models at the cell and tissue scales to expose fundamental arrhythmia vulnerability mechanisms and the complex interactions underlying emergent behaviors. Human clinical data were used for model validation and showed excellent agreement, demonstrating the feasibility of this new approach for cardiotoxicity prediction.

In this renewal application, we propose to greatly extend this approach to include prediction of the interaction between cardiac channel gating and drugs, as well as the inclusion of adrenergic receptor interactions with drugs. Another essential aspect of safety pharmacology is the development of new approaches that allow more efficient drug design, screening and prediction of cardiotoxicity. We will therefore seek to develop, extend and apply a variety of machine learning and deep learning approaches to improve drug discovery by predicting proarrhythmia from drug chemistry, with an efficient process that identifies drug congeners via machine learning to maximize therapeutic benefit and minimize side effects. Finally, we propose to classify drugs into categories based on proarrhythmia risk in normal and diseased virtual tissue settings. The multiscale model for the prediction of cardiopharmacology that we will develop in this application will be applied to projects demonstrating its usefulness for assessing the efficacy or toxicity of drug treatments in the complex physiological system of the heart.

Up to 75% of antibiotic use in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) is inappropriate or unnecessary. In response, and because of increasing evidence of poor outcomes associated with suboptimal antibiotic prescribing in the long-term care setting, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) now require LTCFs to implement and maintain antimicrobial stewardship programs as a condition of participation. A major challenge to improving antibiotic use in LTCFs is that 40-50% of LTCF antibiotic use is initiated in acute care hospitals before LTCF admission. Furthermore, an estimated 70% of antibiotic prescribing at hospital discharge is inappropriate, and patients prescribed antibiotics at discharge to an LTCF often lack information about the antibiotic indication, duration, and culture results in their discharge summaries.

At present, no interventions specifically target antibiotic prescribing at discharge from acute care hospitals to LTCFs. Our long-term goal is to improve antibiotic prescribing in LTCFs and the associated patient and resident outcomes. In this application, we will use a mixed-methods approach to develop an evidence-based intervention bundle targeting high-value areas to optimize antibiotic prescribing at discharge from hospitals to LTCFs. High-value targets for intervention will be prevalent, modifiable, associated with poor clinical outcomes, and not currently addressed in standard practice. We propose the following specific aims.

Specific Aim 1: Identify high-value targets of interventions to optimize antibiotic prescribing on transition from hospitals to LTCFs. We will conduct two multi-center retrospective cohort studies: 1) a hospital-focused study of patients discharged from a network of academic, regional, and community hospitals in Oregon, Washington, and Wisconsin, and 2) an LTCF-focused study of residents admitted from hospitals to 23 LTCFs in Oregon, California, Nevada, and Wisconsin.

Specific Aim 2: Identify and describe barriers and facilitators of interventions to optimize antibiotic prescribing on transition from hospitals to LTCFs. We will conduct in-depth qualitative interviews with hospital and LTCF healthcare providers, nurses, and administrators.

Specific Aim 3: Develop and refine candidate interventions to address the high-value targets and gaps identified in Aims 1 and 2. We will use a collaborative process with key hospital and LTCF stakeholders to refine the candidate interventions and sequentially test the acceptability of the intervention bundle.
